title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
We reviewed the portfolio workflow, took a quiz, and began working with two core tools for public-policy data analysis:

dplyr, an R package for transforming tables.
tidycensus, an R package for downloading Census and American Community Survey (ACS) data.

The class connected data manipulation with an important data source: Census geography and ACS estimates.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
We reviewed the portfolio workflow, took a quiz, and began working with two core tools for public-policy data analysis:

tidycensus, an R package for downloading Census and American Community Survey (ACS) data.

The class connected data manipulation with an important data source: Census geography and ACS estimates.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Key Concepts

An object stores a value or a table in R.
A function takes an input, does something, and returns an output.
A tibble is a modern kind of data frame: observations are rows and variables are columns.
dplyr verbs make table operations readable: filter rows, select columns, create variables, sort rows, and summarize groups.
The Decennial Census counts the population every ten years; the ACS is a continuous sample survey that provides estimates and uncertainty.
A GEOID is a geographic identifier and should be stored as text so its leading zeros are preserved.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Note

1. Where R code lives
Code typed directly into the Console is useful for trying something out, but it disappears from the record of the project. Save reusable code in an R script, or put code and its results in a Quarto code chunk.
Console      -> temporary experiment
.R script    -> reusable code
.qmd file    -> writing + code + rendered results
For example, this line creates an object named result:
result <- filter(counties, population > 50000)
result                  object that will hold the output
<-                      assignment operator
filter()                function (a dplyr verb)
counties                input data
population > 50000      condition / argument
# comment               explanation for people; R does not run it
<- is the usual R style for assignment. = can also assign an object in many simple cases, but it is also used to name function arguments, so using <- makes the intent clearer.


2. Packages: install once, load each session
A package is a collection of functions. Install it once on a computer, then load it again whenever a new R session needs it.
# Run once on a computer
install.packages("dplyr")
install.packages("tidycensus")

# Run at the start of each new R session
library(dplyr)
library(tidycensus)


3. Tibbles and dplyr verbs
A tibble is a table. Each row is one observation, and each column is one variable.



name
income
moe
moe_pct




Adams
78,975
3,334
9


Berks
74,617
1,191
12


Bucks
104,200
1,502
11



The most common dplyr verbs are:
filter()                    keep rows that meet a condition
select()                    keep or reorder columns
mutate()                    add or change a computed column
arrange()                   reorder rows; use desc() for descending order
group_by() + summarize()    turn many rows into group-level summaries
For example, first keep counties whose margin of error is more than 10%; then sort them from highest to lowest; then keep only the name and percentage:
step_1 <- filter(counties, moe_pct > 10)
step_2 <- arrange(step_1, desc(moe_pct))
step_3 <- select(step_2, name, moe_pct)
The resulting table is:



name
moe_pct




Berks
12


Bucks
11



The same work can be written as a pipeline. Both %>% and |> mean roughly “and then.”
new_data <- counties |>
  filter(moe_pct > 10) |>
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) |>
  select(name, moe_pct)


4. Decennial Census and the ACS
The two Census Bureau products answer different questions:









Product
What it provides
Geography
Important limitation




Decennial Census
A count of the full population every 10 years
Down to Census blocks
Does not provide the full range of social and economic characteristics


American Community Survey (ACS)
Annual estimates for income, education, housing, commuting, poverty, and more
ACS 5-year data reach tracts and block groups
Results are estimates, so they include uncertainty



For ACS data, keep two values in mind:
Estimate (E)          the estimated value
Margin of Error (M)   the uncertainty around that estimate
The ACS uses a sample rather than a complete count. Its 1-year product is the most current, but it is available only for larger areas; the lecture used a 65,000-person threshold. Its 5-year product combines five years of responses, works for nearly all geographies, and is generally the appropriate choice for Census tract or block-group analysis.
ACS 1-year  -> more current; fewer and usually larger geographies
ACS 5-year  -> less current; more precise for small-area analysis
ACS 3-year estimates have been discontinued. A 2016 ACS 5-year estimate, for example, pools responses collected from 2012 through 2016.


5. Census geography and GEOIDs
The basic Census geographic hierarchy is:
state -> county -> Census tract -> block group -> Census block
Census tracts are useful approximations of neighborhoods, but they are not official neighborhood boundaries. They are designed to contain roughly 1,200 to 8,000 people (with an ideal size of about 4,000), and their boundaries can change over time. When comparing historical tract data, resources such as NHGIS and the Longitudinal Tract Database (LTDB) can help.
A GEOID uniquely identifies a geographic unit. For example, the Census tract GEOID 42101000100 contains:



Part
Digits
Meaning




42
2
Pennsylvania


101
3
Philadelphia County


000100
6
Census tract



GEOIDs are identifiers, not quantities. Store them as character strings:
"01001"  # correct: leading zero is preserved
1001     # not appropriate for an identifier: the leading zero is lost


6. ACS variable codes and tidycensus
ACS variables follow a structured naming system. In B19013_001E:



Part
Meaning




B19013
table number


001
line number within the table


E
estimate (M means margin of error)



Use load_variables() to search the available variables for a given year and survey:
library(tidycensus)

variables_2023 <- load_variables(2023, "acs5", cache = TRUE)
get_acs() downloads data. This example retrieves Pennsylvania county-level median household income and total population from the 2023 ACS 5-year release:
library(tidycensus)

data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(
    median_income = "B19013_001",
    total_population = "B01003_001"
  ),
  state = "PA",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)


7. Long (tidy) and wide data
The same information can be arranged in two useful ways:








Format
One row represents
Best for




Long / tidy
one geography x one variable
cleaning, filtering, visualization, and repeated operations across variables


Wide
one geographic unit
analysis, modeling, and joining with other datasets



For example, long data have a variable, estimate, and moe column, so Adams County appears once per ACS variable. Wide data keep one Adams County row but use separate columns such as median_incomeE and total_populationE.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.






TipDelete this box



Rewrite the paragraph below in your own words once you’ve picked your state and variable. Two or three sentences saying what you’re looking at and why.


In this analysis, I look at [YOUR VARIABLE] across counties in [YOUR STATE], and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

Choosing what to measure






NoteInstructions — delete this box



Pick a state and a variable. Anything except Pennsylvania and median household income, which we did in class.
Some variables that work well:

vars <- load_variables(2023, "acs5")
View(vars)

Pulling the data

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variable,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

Let’s look at what came back.

dim(county_data)
head(county_data)

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = ___ / ___ * 100)







NoteDelete this box



Fill in the two blanks. You want: how big is the margin of error, relative to the estimate, as a percentage?


Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)







TipDelete this box



Write a sentence or two naming the least reliable county and its moe_pct.


[Which county has the largest margin of error relative to its estimate? How large is it?]

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)







NoteDelete this box



Those cutoffs (5% and 10%) are a bit of a judgment call, not a law of nature. If almost every county lands in one category, adjust them so the split is informative for your variable — then say in your writing that you changed them and why. (I have a feeling for county-level, you may end up in high confidence everywhere - is smaller geographies where it really shows up. So feel free to change those numbers around a bit)


[How many counties fall into each category?]

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)







NoteDelete this box



Notice the column names: myvarE, myvarM, popE, popM. The E and M suffixes are estimate and margin of error.



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(___) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(___)
  )







NoteDelete this box



Two blanks. What are you grouping by? What are you averaging?








TipDelete this box



This table is the heart of the assignment. Describe what it shows in two or three sentences.


[What is the average population of high-confidence counties versus low-confidence counties? Is there a pattern?]

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy






ImportantInstructions — delete this box



Write 200–250 words.
Address all three:

Which communities in your state do we know the least about? Name specific counties from your results.
Why? Connect the pattern to how the ACS actually works — it’s a sample, and smaller places yield smaller samples.
What could go wrong? Imagine a state agency allocating funding using your variable, treating every county’s number as equally certain. Who is likely to be hurt, and how?

Use your own numbers.


[Your 200–250 word reflection goes here.]

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Optional challenges - For those craving more
text:
Optional challenges - For those craving more






NoteDelete this box



None of these are graded. There are no extra points. A complete, well-written assignment earns a 2 either way.
They’re here for anyone who finished the above and found it straightforward. Pick one (or more) that interests you.

Propagate the margin of error. If you compute a derived value — a percentage, a ratio, a sum — its uncertainty depends on the uncertainty of its inputs, and you can’t just carry the original MOE along. The Census Bureau publishes formulas for this, and tidycensus implements them: moe_sum(), moe_prop(), moe_ratio(). Compute something derived, and get its margin of error right.
Parameterize the report. Add params: to the YAML so the state is an input rather than hard-coded, and the same file regenerates for any state. Render it from the terminal with quarto render assignment2.qmd -P state:NY.
Write a function and iterate. Wrap the data pull in a function, then use purrr::map_dfr() to run it across several states at once. Does the small-places-are-noisier pattern hold everywhere, or are some states different?
Change the geographic scale. Run the same variable at geography = "tract" inside one county. Compare the margins of error to what you saw at county level. What does that imply about the resolution at which you can actually trust ACS data?

If you try one, add a short section describing what you did and what you found.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
Key Concepts
Three places a file can live:

My computer — where I edit
GitHub.com — where it’s stored
My live site — what the world sees

The loop: Edit → Save → Render → Commit → Push → wait → refresh

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
Note

1. What is a website?
In class, we described a website as two things working together:
a folder of .html files + a computer/server that is always online
For this course portfolio, those two parts are handled by Quarto and GitHub Pages:
Quarto        -> creates the .html files
GitHub Pages  -> hosts the website for free
The basic idea is:
.qmd file that I write
        -> Quarto renders it
        -> .html webpage
        -> GitHub Pages publishes it
This means I usually work on the source file, not the final webpage file.


2. Quarto
Quarto is the tool that turns a .qmd file into a webpage.
The simplified relationship is:
.qmd (you write) -> Quarto (machine) -> .html (webpage)
The action that makes this happen is Render:
.qmd -> Render -> .html


3. What happens during Render?
When I click Render, Quarto reads the file from top to bottom.
It does roughly this:

Reads the .qmd file.
Finds code chunks.
Sends R code to R.
Gets results back from R.
Glues text, code, and results into HTML.

This is why Render is more than saving. Save keeps changes on my computer; Render rebuilds the webpage output.


4. Anatomy of a .qmd file
A .qmd file usually has three parts:
YAML header + Markdown text + R code chunks

YAML header
The YAML header goes at the very top of the file and is surrounded by ---:
---
title: "Week 1 Reflection"
description: "My first weekly note"
date: 2026-08-28
---
It tells Quarto information about the page, such as the title, description, and date.
Important YAML rules:

It must be at the very top of the file.
The opening and closing --- lines matter.
Colons need a space after them.
Dates should use the YYYY-MM-DD format.
Quotation marks should be plain English quotation marks.



Markdown text
Markdown text is the written content of the page:
## Reflection

This week, I learned how to set up RStudio and Quarto.

### Smaller Section

- First point
- Second point
Markdown is where I write headings, paragraphs, lists, links, and notes.


R code chunks
R code chunks are sections where R code can be run. A chunk begins with three backticks followed by {r}, contains R code, and ends with three backticks:

```{r}
summary(cars)
```

If I want to show code but not run it, I can use the eval: false option:

```{r}
#| eval: false
summary(cars)
```




5. Source files and output files
The most important file rule is to edit source files, not output files.
Source files are files I write:
index.qmd
about.qmd
weekly-notes/week-01.qmd
assignments/*.qmd
_quarto.yml
Output files are files the machine makes:
docs/index.html
docs/about.html
docs/weekly-notes/week-01.html
the rest of the docs/ folder
The rule is:
Edit the source files. Do not edit or move the output files.


6. Files and folders
The guiding question from the note is:
Who is this file for?
Files for me to write:
index.qmd
about.qmd
weekly-notes/*.qmd
assignments/*.qmd
Files or folders for tools:
_quarto.yml     settings for the whole website
.Rproj          tells RStudio this folder is a project
.gitignore      tells Git what not to track
.Renviron       stores secrets for R, such as API keys
docs/           website output for the internet
_freeze/        Quarto cache or frozen output


7. Index
On the web, index.html is the default page for a folder. If I ask for a folder URL, the server usually gives me that folder’s index.html.
Example:
website folder URL -> index.html inside that folder
For the portfolio website:
index.qmd -> Quarto render -> docs/index.html
That is why the homepage source file is named index.qmd.


8. Git / GitHub.com / GitHub Desktop
These three are related, but they mean different things:
Git             version tracker
GitHub.com      website that stores a copy of my folder
GitHub Desktop  buttons that tell Git what to do
Git is mostly invisible and runs on my computer. GitHub.com stores the online copy. GitHub Desktop is the app I use to tell Git when to commit and push.


9. Commit and push
Commit and push are two different actions:
Commit = save a labeled snapshot on my computer
Push   = send that snapshot to GitHub.com
Commit happens locally. Push sends the committed version online.


10. R Script
An R script is different from a .qmd file.
R script = code only
.qmd     = writing + code + results
An R script is useful as a sandbox for trying code. A .qmd file is useful when I want to combine explanation, code, and output in a webpage or report.
